newsitem.title: USA: Foodservice firm consolidation seen accelerating.
newsitem.headline: Foodservice firm consolidation seen accelerating.

text.p: Consolidation of the fragmented U.S. foodservice industry is expected to accelerate following the $1.4 billion JP Foodservices Inc / Rykoff-Sexton Inc merger, analysts said.
Together, the two companies would hold four percent of the $140 billion industry, still a far second to industry giant Sysco Corp's 10 percent, they said.

"The merger of the number three player (Rykoff-Sexton) and the number five player (JP) will create a strong number two broadline foodservice distributor with a complete national presence," Morgan Stanley Dean Witter analyst John Renwick said in a research note.

Jim Miller, chairman of JP, said in an interview with Reuters after the deal was announced Monday that the foodservice industry "is about 15 years behind the retail (food) industry, when regional chains like Safeway (Inc ) bought up ma and pa grocieries."

"It is a scale-driven, cost-driven business, moving toward consolidation. It is a merger that had to happen," said Miller, who will be chairman and chief executive of the merged company, with about $5.2 billion in annual revenues.

Analyst Ken Shea of Standard & Poor's said, "I am surprised (a large merger in the industry) has taken so long. Sysco is the leader in an extremely fragmented market, so it does not surprise me there is a consolidation wave. JP and Rykoff are near the top of the industry, but will not dent Sysco because it is so large."
Morgan Stanley's Renwick called the transaction "a substantial long-term positive."

"In addition to the existing growth factors, including growth in consumer expenditures for food prepared away from home, market share gains in local markets and potential future accretive acquisitions, the proposed merger introduces another vehicle for growth and earnings surprises -- consolidation savings," Renwick said in the note.

"In the end, the combined entity will be a bigger, stronger company with a nine to 10 percent top-line growth rate, improved EBIT (earnings before income tax) margins and a lower cost of capital," Renwick wrote.

Under the agreement, unanimously approved by both companies' directors, JP and Rykoff would merge in a tax-free exchange of shares under which Rykoff holders would get 0.84 JP share for each Rykoff share held.
JP also would assume $700 million in Rykoff debt.

Shareholders representing about 36 percent of Rykoff have agreed to back the deal, and there is no share-price collar in the pact, a provision that typically would triggers a renegotiation of merger terms if the stocks of merger parties rose or fell sharply.
In afternoon NYSE trade, Rykoff shares were up 3-11/16 to to 23-5/16, easing off an earlier year-high of 23-3/8. Sysco slipped 1/8 to 36-7/8.
